query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A single thermal post‐treatment in a controlled, oxidizing and humid atmosphere can transform the as‐synthesized near‐equiatomic multi‐principal-element automotive alloy catalyst to form a nanoporous, high‐entropy oxide surface layer that stabilizes minimal platinum-group metal (PGM) sites. This engineered surface will simultaneously lower the light‐off temperature for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation, enhance resistance to common exhaust poisons like H2O and NO, and markedly improve long-term durability under realistic engine aging conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst containing primarily non‐noble metals (e.g., Cu, Ni, etc.) with minimal PGM content.
generation.intervention: Apply a dedicated thermal post‐treatment (annealing) in an oxidizing atmosphere containing controlled amounts of water vapor at moderate temperatures to induce in situ formation of a nanoporous high‐entropy oxide layer on the catalyst surface.
generation.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust conditions including transient and low-temperature operation (targeting complete oxidation below 150 °C) in an oxygen‐rich environment with typical levels of moisture (e.g., 10 vol% vapor) and NO. Durability should be assessed under accelerated thermal aging (up to ~850 °C with moisture) and cycling conditions mimicking high-mileage operation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a nanoporous high‐entropy oxide layer—characterized by stable grain boundaries and a preserved porous framework—will mediate the improved stabilization of sub‐nanometric PGM sites and active metal centers.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of the freshly generated oxide layer lowers the surface free energy, which suppresses sintering of the few PGM sites and other active metals. The nanoporous structure also minimizes blockage by poisoning species (H2O and NO) by facilitating continuous reactant access and efficient removal of reaction by‐products, thereby enhancing catalytic kinetics and endurance during thermal cycling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the post-treated catalyst is expected to display a substantially lower oxidation temperature (light‐off below 150 °C), improved resistance to deactivation by water and NO, and stable catalytic performance over long-term aging tests—all while preserving very low platinum-group-metal usage.
generation.baseline: The unmodified near‐equiatomic catalyst suffers from higher light‐off temperatures, rapid deactivation in the presence of H2O and NO, and a marked degradation in activity over extended thermal and mechanical cycling.
generation.boundary: The positive effects are anticipated under automotive-relevant exhaust conditions (e.g., lean, oxygen-rich, transient low-temperature operation with up to 10 vol% water vapor and trace NO) and up to modest thermal aging (~850 °C). Effects under extreme conditions beyond these parameters remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing parameters (temperature, duration, and vapor concentration) needed to reliably produce the desired nanoporous oxide layer require further specification. Moreover, interactions with a full range of real-world exhaust contaminants beyond H2O and NO, and the exact longevity under varied transient cycles, still carry uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst: one subjected to the proposed thermal post‐treatment (in an oxidizing, humid atmosphere) and one kept as the untreated control. Test both catalysts under simulated automotive exhaust conditions (transient operation at temperatures below 150 °C, in an oxygen-rich atmosphere with ~10 vol% water vapor and trace NO) and subject them to accelerated aging cycles (e.g., thermal aging up to 850 °C under humid conditions followed by cyclic operation).
measurements: Light‐off temperature (T10 and T50) for CO/hydrocarbon oxidation
CO conversion rate and complete conversion temperature under realistic exhaust gas composition
Catalyst poisoning resistance (activity retention in the presence of water and NO)
Long-term durability metrics (activity retention over 338 h and across multiple reaction cycles)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post-treated catalyst fails to demonstrate statistically significant improvements (e.g., lower light-off temperatures, enhanced resistance to H2O and NO poisoning, and better long-term stability) compared to the untreated baseline catalyst under the defined test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractEnhancing the activity and stability of earth‐abundant, heterogeneous catalysts remains a key challenge, requiring new materials design strategies to replace platinum‐group metals. Herein, it is demonstrated that increasing the configurational disorder of spinel metal oxides (M3O4, where M is a combination of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn) leads to significant improvements in carbon monoxide (CO) oxidation performance. A substantial 63% decrease in the T10 value (temperature to reach 10% CO oxidation) is observed by systematically increasing the number of first‐row transition metals within the spinel oxide. Long‐term stability studies reveal that the most disordered 7‐metal spinel oxide exhibited superior resistance to catalyst deactivation compared to the 4‐metal variant, showing a decrease in activity of only 4.7% versus 12.2% during 14 h of operation. A solventless thermolysis approach is developed to synthesize a series of medium entropy spinel oxide (MESO) and high entropy spinel oxides (HESOs) from discrete, air‐stable molecular precursors. cited_evidence.text: These results underline the exceptional thermal stability of Pt nanoparticles, which is attributed to the high‐entropy effect. As shown in Figure 4g, the Pt/HEO‐850 °C catalyst demonstrated excellent stability during CO oxidation at 210 °C, maintaining consistent activity over 338 h with ignorable decline (Table S3, Supporting Information). The Pt/HEO‐850 °C demonstrates a slight decline (2.4%) in the 30‐h running with a low deactivation rate constant (k d) of 3.2 × 10−3 h−1, compared with recent Pt‐based catalysts (Figure 4h).[  ] This result exceeds the thermal stability conventional catalysts, showcasing its superior sinter‐resistance. To simulate hydrothermal conditions, vapor was introduced during testing, and even after 35 consecutive cycles, ignorable performance declines were observed (Figure 4i). In the 36th cycle, the porous structure remained intact, with the Pt nanoparticle size increasing only by 0.1–2.7 nm (Figures S36 and S37, Supporting Information). The durability of Pt/HEO in moisture‐rich environments, such as automotive exhaust systems, underscores its potential as a highly reliable catalyst for CO oxidation.
